extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy, aesthetics, and music theory (scholars interested in metaphysics, ethics, and the philosophy of art)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length philosophical exposition treating (1) aesthetics and music (dissonance/consonance, keys, temperament) and (2) metaphysical reflections on death, the will to live, and the indestructibility of the true nature. Intended as part of a systematic philosophical work rather than a how-to or policy guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternation of dissonance and consonance in music
rubrics_metrics.description: The harmonious sequence of chords consists of the correct alternation of dissonance and consonance; a succession of merely consonant chords would be satiating, wearisome, and empty, like the languor produced by the satisfaction of all wishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that dissonances must be introduced (though they disquiet us) only to be resolved in consonances with proper preparation; compares musical alternation to the life of the will (dissatisfaction and satisfaction). The passage emphasizes variety and prepared resolution as compositional necessities to avoid tedium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension as a means to heighten satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspension is a dissonance which delays the final consonance, which is awaited with certainty; thus the longing for it is strengthened, and its appearance satisfies all the more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames suspension as analogous to poetic rhyme and to the will's heightened satisfaction through delay; presents suspension as an intentional compositional device to increase affective impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete cadence requires the dominant seventh prior to resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete cadence requires the preceding chord of the seventh on the dominant; because the most deeply felt satisfaction and the most entire relief can only follow the most earnest longing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a concrete rule of tonal practice tying musical effect (heightened relief) to harmonic procedure (dominant seventh preparation). This is presented as normative for producing the strongest cadential satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two fundamental chords underlie harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: In the whole of music there are really only two fundamental chords, the dissonant chord of the seventh and the consonant triad, to which all chords that occur can be referred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offers a reductionist account of harmony that maps musical structure to the will's states (dissatisfaction and satisfaction); treats other chords as derivable from these two foundational types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major and minor correspond to general moods
rubrics_metrics.description: Music has two general keys, the major (serenity, or at least healthiness) and the minor (sadness, or even oppression), and it must always be in one of the two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims an intrinsic psychological correspondence between key and basic moods; cites cultural tendencies (northern nations, Russians, French allegro in minor) as exemplars. Uses the minor as a near-universal sign of pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal temperament introduces unavoidable impurity
rubrics_metrics.description: The unavoidable impurity of every harmonic system (referred to earlier) is introduced by the equal temperament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the key-note is changed and intervals change value, notes must assume different 'roles' like actors ill-suited to some rôles; equal temperament’s compromises are likened to this unavoidable impurity in harmonic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: To understand the author's philosophy one must read all of it
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever wishes to make himself acquainted with my philosophy shall read every line of me; whoever wishes to learn from me and understand me must leave nothing unread that I have written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues he writes little but with reflection and that his ideas are not dispersed across many compendia; selective reading will miss essential connections—hence a methodological requirement for study (comprehensive reading) to fairly judge or understand the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear of death derives from the will to live, not from knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The fear of death is a priori only the reverse side of the will to live; it proceeds entirely and alone from the blind will, of which everything living is filled. Knowledge is originally foreign to the will and can combat this blind attachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes willing (blind, a priori attachment to life) from knowing (which reveals life's worthlessness); explains how knowledge can diminish fear of death, while the will produces the overwhelming attachment to life and fear of annihilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: From the standpoint of knowledge there is no reason to fear death
rubrics_metrics.description: From the standpoint of knowledge there appears absolutely no reason to fear death: consciousness is not concerned by death (when we are death is not, and when death is we are not); not-being after death is no different in kind from not-being before birth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Epicurean and Kantian motifs, analogies with sleep and fainting, and empirical observations (testimonies about painless loss of consciousness) to argue that death is not an evil for consciousness; treats pre-birth nonexistence as a consoling analogue to post-death nonexistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death, subjectively, concerns only the vanishing of consciousness; organismal destruction affects the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjectively, death consists only in the moment when consciousness vanishes because the activity of the brain ceases; the destruction of the organism is really the will itself exhibiting itself as body and is what we feel as loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes immediate subjective experience (loss of consciousness, often painless) from subsequent physical disintegration; uses fainting, drowning, and death from old age as empirical illustrations of the subjective quality of dying and the gradual fading in senescence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indestructibility of our true nature argued from permanence of matter and forces
rubrics_metrics.description: The inmost principle of life (the vital force) may be conceived as a force of nature and thus remains untouched by change of forms and states; the permanence and ubiquity of natural forces and matter afford evidence (in image or simile) of the indestructibility of our true nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues by analogy: permanence of matter and continuity of natural forces suggest an imperishableness of the thing-in-itself (the will). The author acknowledges this is not the kind of proof religious consolations ask for but regards it as a philosophically grounded indication of indestructibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical viewpoints (materialism vs. idealism) are one-sided but relatively true
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistent materialism and absolute idealism are each exceedingly one-sided comprehensions, and therefore, in spite of their opposition, they are all true each from a definite point of view; only the highest standpoint can survey them and recognize both their relative truth and falseness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames competing metaphysical systems as perspectival truths; recommends elevation to a higher standpoint to see their partial truths and limitations. Presented as methodological guidance for philosophical synthesis rather than an empirical criterion.
